source.title: Collective Phenomena in the LiHoxY1−xF4 Quantum Ising Magnet: Recent Progress and Open Questions

accepted.question_text: What is the actual low-temperature magnetic-domain structure of pure LiHoF4, an insulating dipolar Ising ferromagnet whose Ho3+ moments order below about 1.53 K along the crystalline c axis, and can experiments verify the predicted rich structure in which the ground-state domains consist of parallel antiferromagnetically aligned sheets whose sizes and possible branching depend on demagnetization effects and sample geometry?

evidence.quote: For LiHoF4, the ground state domain configuration is expected to consist of parallel antiferromagnetically aligned sheets [17, 18, 19]. The size of the domains increases with decreasing demagnetization factor and, in the limit of infinitely long thin samples, a state of uniform magnetization is possible.

Also, for thick samples, a branched pattern is predicted in the domain structure for a dipolar Ising ferromagnet [17, 18]. LiHoF4 is an excellent test case for theories of domain formation due to the availability of an accurate microscopic model of the material (see below). It remains an open experimental challenge to verify the nature of the predicted rich domain structure.

accepted.question_text: Why is the ferromagnetic ordered state of pure LiHoF4 unexpectedly stable against a weak transverse magnetic field Bx, even near the classical transition temperature Tc = 1.53 K, when the measured Tc(Bx) phase boundary rises much more steeply than predictions from the effective transverse-field Ising model, and are magnetostriction, neglected terms in the effective model, or anisotropic exchange interactions responsible?

evidence.quote: Notwithstanding the importance of hyperfine effects at low temperature, one notes that even close to the classical critical temperature of Tc = 1.53 K, the experimental [22] phase boundary rises much more steeply than in the model of Eq. (2) [20, 21].

The reason for this stability of the ordered state with respect to weak Bx is an open question. Possible explanations include magnetostriction effects, small terms that are neglected in the effective model of Eq. (2) (see Refs. [20, 21] for a discussion of those terms) or anisotropic exchange terms, such as Juvex(rij)JuiJvj, altogether ignored in the microscopic model of Eq. (1).

The two foremost outstanding questions are whether a thermodynamic spin glass phase survives in the limit of high dilution of the magnetic Ho3+ ions and the reason for the unexpected stability of the ferromagnetic ground state of pure LiHoF4 with respect to an applied transverse field.

accepted.question_text: What quantitatively accurate role do Ho hyperfine interactions play in the global concentration-temperature-transverse-field phase diagram of LiHoxY1−xF4, especially in regimes where the ferromagnetic or spin-glass critical temperature drops below roughly 0.5 K and the hyperfine interaction inhibits quantum fluctuations and strongly renormalizes the critical transverse field?
accepted.context_brief: Hyperfine effects in the global phase diagram

evidence.quote: As the critical (ferromagnetic or spin glass) temperature decreases, and drops below approximately 0.5 K, the role of the hyperfine interaction in inhibiting quantum fluctuations and strongly renormalizing the critical transverse field cannot be ignored [32, 33].

While progress has been achieved as to how to proceed [33], work does remain to be done to investigate via quantitatively accurate calculations (e.g. quantum Monte Carlo simulations) the role of hyperfine interactions on the global x − T − Bx phase diagram of LiHoxY1−xF4.

accepted.question_text: In diluted LiHoxY1−xF4 subject to a nonzero transverse magnetic field Bx, do the correlated internal random fields h_i^z induced by Bx have the same effect as uncorrelated random fields in the simplest transverse-field Ising model, namely destroying zero-temperature quantum criticality and driving the system toward a fluctuationless classical zero-temperature random-field fixed point?
accepted.context_brief: Correlated random fields and quantum criticality

evidence.quote: In the context of the physics of induced random fields, it is worthwhile to note that theoretical work predicts that in the simplest TFIM of Eq. (3), the addition of uncorrelated random fields should destroy the zero temperature quantum criticality and drive the renormalization group flow towards the fluctuationless (classical) zero temperature random field fixed point [68].
It would be interesting to investigate the implication of that result for the correlated hzi random fields discussed above and that exist in LiHoxY1−xF4 in nonzero Bx.

accepted.question_text: Do transverse-field-induced random fields in diluted ferromagnetic LiHoxY1−xF4, for example at Ho concentration x = 0.44, produce Griffiths singularity effects in the paramagnetic regime just above the ferromagnetic transition temperature Tc, and what systematic experimental investigation is needed to test the claimed susceptibility-scaling behavior?

evidence.quote: Finally, we note that the presence of induced random fields has been invoked to interpret the transverse field and temperature dependence (e.g. scaling behavior) of the magnetic susceptibility in LiHoxY1−xF4 (x = 0.44).

In particular, these random fields have been postulated to give rise to Griffiths' singularity effects in the paramagnetic regime at temperatures just above Tc [69]. It would be useful to explore this claim further.
In fact, a systematic experimental investigation of the fascinating physics of random field systems in the diluted ferromagnetic regime of LiHoxY1−xF4 is probably warranted.

accepted.question_text: What is the magnetic state of LiHoxY1−xF4 in the high-dilution, zero-transverse-field regime, especially for Ho concentration x < 0.1 and more broadly for x ≲ 0.25: does a thermodynamic spin-glass phase survive toward x = 0+, is the state instead an unusual antiglass or quantum-disordered spin-liquid-like phase, or is there no spin-glass phase at all in this concentration range?

evidence.quote: Whether the dipolar SG exists down to x = 0+ or an exotic quantum disordered ‘antiglass’ (AG) phase occurs at x > 0 (red line segment) is not yet resolved and is the subject of much controversy.

The single most important open question is the nature of the magnetic state in the limit of high dilution (x < 0.1). Is it a traditional spin glass, as suggested by the recent measurements of Quilliam et al. [79] or is it an unusual antiglass spin liquid [74, 75, 76, 77]?
One may even ask whether there is a spin glass phase at all for x ≲ 0.25 [51, 52, 59].

The two foremost outstanding questions are whether a thermodynamic spin glass phase survives in the limit of high dilution of the magnetic Ho3+ ions and the reason for the unexpected stability of the ferromagnetic ground state of pure LiHoF4 with respect to an applied transverse field.

accepted.question_text: Why do technically demanding AC-susceptibility and specific-heat experiments on high-dilution LiHoxY1−xF4 disagree about whether the system shows conventional spin-glass freezing or unusual antiglass behavior, particularly between the earlier measurements of Reich, Ghosh, and collaborators and the later measurements of Quilliam and collaborators?

evidence.quote: Recent measurements by Quilliam et al. [79] contradict the earlier results [74, 75, 76] and find that the frequency distribution of χ”, broadens as the temperature is reduced also in the high dilution limit (x = 4.5%) as shown in the left panel of Fig. 2.

Furthermore, the specific heat data reported in Ref. [80] do not display any of the unusual features that were previously interpreted as a telltale signature of entangled magnetic moments within a quantum disordered antiglass state [77].

The reason for the difference between the AC susceptibility and specific heat experimental results of Refs. [74, 75, 76, 77] and Refs. [79, 80] remains an open question. Due to the very slow dynamics, all these measurements are technically very demanding.

accepted.question_text: How do sample-quality factors in highly diluted LiHoxY1−xF4, such as impurities and the homogeneity of Y3+ substitutional disorder, affect the observed low-temperature magnetic state and the interpretation of spin-glass versus antiglass behavior?

evidence.quote: The ‘sample quality’ (e.g. impurity, homogeneous Y3+ disorder, etc) may be of importance in this highly dilute limit and this issue should be examined carefully.

accepted.question_text: Do sample shape and demagnetization effects influence whether a spin-glass phase exists in highly diluted LiHoxY1−xF4, even though such effects are expected not to determine the existence of the spin-glass phase?

evidence.quote: Sample shape and demagnetization effects should not affect the existence of the spin glass phase, but this should nevertheless be investigated.

accepted.question_text: Can the hole-burning response and persistent oscillations reported in highly diluted LiHoxY1−xF4 be independently reproduced, and if so, what unusual low-temperature physical state do these effects indicate?

evidence.quote: The manifestation of dissipationless dynamics of a broad inhomogeneous distribution of quantum oscillators within the inferred antiglass regime was further demonstrated through (i) hole burning in the AC susceptibility spectrum [76] and, (ii) perhaps most interestingly, via the observation of persistent oscillations for up to 30 seconds after an external AC field is turned off [76].
The hole-burning and persistent oscillations observed by Ghosh et al. [76] are also indicative of a very unusual physical state, yet they have not been reported or reproduced by another group.

accepted.question_text: For diluted dipolar Ising models intended to describe LiHoxY1−xF4, can larger classical Monte Carlo simulations bring finite-size corrections under control, reconcile the different spin-glass correlation-length crossings along the a and c axes, and thereby determine the finite-temperature spin-glass transition more reliably?

evidence.quote: In Ref. [82], a finite-size crossing of ξsg divided by the linear system size L, ξsg/L, is observed, providing good evidence for a finite temperature spin-glass transition, in agreement with the most recent AC susceptibility experiments [79].

However, the critical temperature determined by the crossing of ξsg/L is slightly different for ξsg along the a and c axes. This indicates that the finite size corrections to scaling are not under control for the system sizes considered and simulations on larger system sizes are therefore needed.

accepted.question_text: How can numerical studies of highly diluted LiHoxY1−xF4 go beyond classical Monte Carlo by incorporating hyperfine interactions and off-diagonal pseudospin interactions, despite the sign problem these terms create for quantum Monte Carlo, so that simulations can make more quantitative comparisons with experiments?
accepted.context_brief: Quantum simulations beyond classical Monte Carlo

evidence.quote: On the numerical side, it would be of interest to go beyond the classical Monte Carlo simulations that have so far been applied to the dilute system.

The effects of the hyperfine interactions and off-diagonal interactions between the σi pseudospins are challenging to incorporate in a quantum Monte Carlo simulation since they lead to a sign problem.
Nevertheless, it would be important to invest some effort in this problem in order to achieve more quantitative comparisons with experiments.

accepted.question_text: Can comparative studies of other highly diluted Ising magnetic materials, including diluted spin-ice compounds (DyxY1−x)2Ti2O7 and (HoxY1−x)2Ti2O7 and proposed transverse-field Ising materials HoxY1−x(OH)3 and DyxY1−x(OH)3, clarify the physics responsible for the high-dilution behavior of LiHoxY1−xF4?

evidence.quote: Perhaps the study of other highly diluted Ising magnetic materials could help shed some light on the physics at play in LiHoxY1−xF4.

In this context, a study of the highly diluted Ising spin ice materials (DyxY1−x)2Ti2O7 and (HoxY1−x)2Ti2O7 [81] as well as the proposed HoxY1−x(OH)3 and DyxY1−x(OH)3 TFIM materials [38] to compare with LiHoxY1−xF4 could prove interesting and instructive.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Examples of cornerstone questions in the field of random disordered systems are: Does a transition that is first order in a pure system remains first order in the presence of random disorder? For a second order transition, does an arbitrary small amount of random disorder change the critical exponents and hence modify the universality class? Does the long range order exhibited by a pure system survive arbitrary small random fields conjugate to the order parameter? When the disorder is large enough and the interactions are in strong competition and lead to random frustration, is there a thermodynamic transition at nonzero temperature to a spin glass state? Under what conditions does a random magnet exhibit nonanalytical behavior above its critical temperature, in the so-called Griffiths phase?

evidence.quote: Examples of cornerstone questions in the field of random disordered systems are: Does a transition that is first order in a pure system remains first order in the presence of random disorder [45]? For a second order transition, does an arbitrary small amount of random disorder change the critical exponents and hence modify the universality class [46]? Does the long range order exhibited by a pure system survive arbitrary small random fields conjugate to the order parameter [47]? When the disorder is large enough and the interactions are in strong competition and lead to random frustration, is there a thermodynamic transition at nonzero temperature to a spin glass state [48, 49]? Under what conditions does a random magnet exhibit nonanalytical behavior above its critical temperature, in the so-called Griffiths phase, which is a remnant of the long range order phase displayed by the parent disorder-free system [50]?

needs_review.question_text_raw: What is the mechanism responsible for the fast Bx-induced destruction of the ferromagnetic and spin-glass phases in LiHoxY1−xF4?

evidence.quote: Two questions have received particular attention: (i) is there an antiglass (quantum disordered) phase at low Ho3+ concentration and (ii) what is the mechanism responsible for the fast Bx-induced destruction of the ferromagnetic (0.25 ≲ x < 1) and spin glass (x ≲ 0.25) phases?

Analytical [33, 62, 63, 64, 65] and numerical [62, 63, 64] studies have shown, rather convincingly, that the presence of Bx-induced random fields hzi can explain the two aforementioned puzzles observed in LiHoxY1−xF4 in nonzero Bx, in both the diluted FM regime and in the SG regime.
